top.line: Citizen developers are good news; their apps are briefs
top.para: A conference raised citizen developers as a worry; I think they are among the best things to happen to software. People who know the work, once limited to spreadsheets, can now build applications that are the best briefs ever written. The work is the handover to villagers and town planners, and vaults are a natural carrier.

in-short.line: Not a risk to contain: the spreadsheet grown up
in-short.para: Citizen developers include employees, owners and experts who know the work. They once built spreadsheets and can now build applications, which are working briefs. The real work is the handover from explorers to villagers and town planners, vaults carry these mini apps well, and the shift moves software from rent-seeking to empowerment.

worry.line: Citizen developers are good news, not a cleanup job
worry.para: A speaker framed citizen developers, attributed to AWS, as a problem for IT, though AWS's own definition is neutral and Gartner treats it as a persona. It is a better term than Karpathy's February 2025 vibe coding. It covers employees, business owners and domain experts building what they need.

spreadsheet.line: Error-filled spreadsheets were people's only self-editable tool
spreadsheet.para: Panko found significant errors in 49 of 54 audited spreadsheets, the London Whale model divided by a sum instead of an average, and England's test and trace lost 15,841 cases to a 65,536-row limit. These show how badly technology served people. Now the same people can build full applications.

brief.line: A user-built working app is a brief that runs
brief.para: Requirements documents were always the weakest link, describing something unseen for someone who does not know the work. An app built by the user says exactly what they want and use. The mistake is treating the brief as a product: it is not yet maintained, secured, tested or scalable.

handover.line: The real work is the handover to villagers
handover.para: In Wardley's terms the citizen developer is an explorer finding needs by building. Villagers harden it and town planners scale it, adding security, reliability, observability, cost, documentation and support. Agents make the handover cheap and visible, and cheaper deep review puts security within everyone's reach.

vaults.line: A vault is a versioned, encrypted spreadsheet app
vaults.para: A spreadsheet is a UI and data in one unversioned, emailed file. An sgit vault holds the same mini app and adds commit history, read-only keys, encryption so it can live anywhere, and a clean handover, since the villager clones exactly what the explorer committed. I already work this way.

empowerment.line: Building your own tools replaces rent-seeking with empowerment
empowerment.para: People, companies and countries served badly by rented software can now build what they need, and sovereignty is the ability to move. When users can build, businesses must serve them well enough that they choose to pay. The newsroom's reading meter, where readers pay after reading, tests that model.

limits.line: The quote is untraced; most apps should stay small
limits.para: The AWS attribution came from a speaker, so AWS's own definition is quoted instead. Panko's audits date from 1997 to 2000, most citizen-built apps should stay small, and vaults are one carrier among others; the argument does not depend on them.

sources.line: Sources: AWS, Gartner, Panko, London Whale and Wardley
sources.para: Written from a 14 October 2026 voice memo after a conference, with quotes checked on their pages. Sources include AWS on low-code, Gartner on citizen developers, Wikipedia on vibe coding, The Register on Panko and test and trace, James Kwak on the London Whale, and Simon Wardley.
